abstract_sixth_review: Hyperbolic representation learning rests on a premise we call latent hyperbolicity: standard models are already tree-like because their class geometry scores a low Gromov $\delta$, a measure of tree-likeness that is zero for a tree. That low value is also what a random cloud of the same dimension and spectrum scores, so we build an instrument that reads every score as its excess over 200 such clouds, and add a depth test whose power is measured. We apply it to 12 vision backbones, 6 datasets and 15 text models. On image features, where the premise is read, the calibrated reading is indistinguishable from a random cloud in most cells and small elsewhere. Class centroids do carry structure that a random cloud of the same shape does not, in {{N_GEN}} of 72 model--dataset cells, but so does a star of clusters. The depth test certifies in {{N_IN}} of 12 ImageNet backbones that clusters are oriented toward their hubs, not that the hubs of the frame form a hierarchy: randomizing the orientations removes every verdict, whereas an implanted hierarchy, synthetic or trained in, survives it. No hub hierarchy is found in the nine backbones where the decoupled control detects an implanted one, and the test is blind in the other three. A backbone trained in hyperbolic space, MERU, shows the same structure as its Euclidean twin and lives in the near-flat regime. Across models the trees are moderately shared: the naive comparison manufactures an island, every recipe partially recovers the human taxonomy once the clustering cut is controlled, and the self-supervised tree is angular. Read correctly, foundation models organize classes into clustered structure that is moderately shared and does not converge to one common tree; no hub hierarchy is found where the test has power; and their raw tree-likeness is not evidence for hyperbolic geometry.
